title: Write the sequence before the items
statement: Write the course sequence before items: declare its policy and feed sources to a model in order of authority, never blended, then check the order it proposes against that policy.
detail: A source atom of the reading project's course standard says to author the curriculum graph and lesson sequence before item authoring, so that available questions cannot become the curriculum by accident (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/sources/review-hub/course-insights-d7f57fb/ATOMS.json`). The curriculum BrainLift warns that a model asked for the best sequence without an explicit policy imports its own assumptions, so every output becomes a debate about taste rather than a review against a policy, and it names the policy's parts: the progression spine, the entry assumptions, the prerequisite strictness and the sequencing priority order (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback1/Curriculum & Knowledge BrainLift.md`).
against: The merge attempt shows only that naive merging fails; keeping each state's detail under a shared node is offered as an untested possibility (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0116-graph-architecture-brainlift-core.qmd`). a later project plan proposes training a model on the team's own teaching principles instead, which is untested. A meeting report said the lesson-writing skill now authors all curriculum and content; the project's notes record it as a meeting claim that conflicts with the verified contract of a human-supplied graph, kept but not allowed to override it (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/HOTBUCKET.md`).

evidence.quote: Author the curriculum graph and lesson sequence before item authoring so available questions cannot become the curriculum by accident.
Every output becomes a debate about taste rather than a review against a policy.

At minimum, this means: the progression spine (chronological? spiral? model-building?), the entry assumptions (what do students already know?), the prerequisite strictness (how many hard gates per lesson?), and the sequencing priority order (what wins when constraints conflict?).
the sequence will reflect whatever assumptions the model happens to import
is not synthesis at all; it is compromise
Proper synthesis is staged. Different sources contribute different things and must be processed in order:
Standards set the intended scope. They are the scope authority.
Assessments reveal what counts as acceptable evidence and typical task conditions. They are the evidence authority.
The result was flattened abstractions that lost the specificity needed for teaching.
it proves that naive merging (abstracting away specifics to find a common description) is the wrong approach.
use the standard to constrain scope (what must appear), but apply independent judgement about order, depth, prerequisite structure, and cognitive demand.
Standards constrain scope but do not provide a teachable sequence.
SUPERSEDES conflicting local docs on sequencing/synthesis/spacing
training an LLM specifically on the team's pedagogical principles rather than only using it to generate content
never blend sources in one pass; supply the sequence policy to the model;
sequence judgment is human-supplied
Load the candidate SKILL.md to author a G3 lesson (start from a course-graph unit spec, not ad hoc).

**You cannot outsource sequence judgment to the model** — the human supplies the policy (spine, entry assumptions, prereq strictness, priority order); the model generates an auditable proposal obeying it.
so sequence judgment cannot be outsourced to a generator
Any model-generated sequence is an auditable proposal reviewed against this policy, not against taste.

The model will average conflicts (producing something that matches no source well), import hidden assumptions from lower-authority sources (textbook idiosyncrasies becoming core curriculum), and expand scope without anyone noticing
Stage by authority: **standards = scope authority; assessments = evidence authority; textbooks = representational authority** (may not expand scope without human sign-off).
a text that smuggles new scope fails placement rather than silently widening the theme.
It lets inventory rather than learning dependencies choose the sequence.
Generate artifacts in the order curriculum graph, curriculum outline, lesson plans, then questions for those lessons.
Questions and lessons need the course decisions they are supposed to realize; reversing the order promotes bank accidents into curriculum choices.

When edges conflict, use this priority: 1. Period integrity and factual chronology. 2. Explicit topic/KC scope from v1. 3. Required prerequisite or revisit activation. 4. Reasoning progression and source availability. 5. Pacing preference.
never ask a model to invent the sequence, delete scope to meet pacing, or treat a curriculum edge as a domain fact.
Generate full lessons after that review.
One-pass blending averages conflicts and silently imports lower-authority scope.
If a local asset conflicts with the fingerprinted CED, the CED wins and the conflict is recorded in `CED-LOCAL-RECONCILIATION.md`; do not silently blend the sources.
